title: Design an Ordered Stream
statement:
Build a class `OrderedStream` that is fed `n` (id, value) pairs one at a time, in any order, and gives the values back sorted by id, a piece at a time.

- `OrderedStream(n)` prepares a stream for the ids `1` to `n`. It tracks the smallest id whose value it has not handed back yet, starting at `1`.
- `insert(idKey, value)` stores `value` under `idKey`. Then, starting at that tracked id, it collects the values of consecutive ids that are already stored, in increasing id order, until it reaches an id that is still missing (or passes `n`). It returns the collected list (empty when the tracked id is missing) and moves the tracked id past everything it returned.

Every `idKey` lies between `1` and `n`, no id is inserted twice, and `insert` is called exactly `n` times, so joining all returned lists gives every value ordered by id.
constraints: value contains only lowercase English letters.
Each call to insert uses a different idKey.
insert is called exactly n times.
notes:
## Intuition

The stream can only release values in id order, so all that matters is the first id not yet released. Keep the values in an array indexed by id and a `pointer` to that first unreleased id. After each insertion, walk the pointer forward over every filled slot; whatever it passes is the chunk to return. A slower idea is to rebuild the whole sorted prefix on every call and return only its new part; the pointer avoids that repeated work.

## Approach

1. The constructor makes `values`, an array of `n + 1` empty slots (slot 0 unused), and sets `pointer = 1`.
2. `insert` writes `value` into slot `idKey`.
3. Start an empty `chunk`. While `pointer` is still inside the array and its slot is filled, push that value and advance `pointer`.
4. Return `chunk`. It is empty when the slot at `pointer` is still missing.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 5`, so `values` has slots 1 to 5 and `pointer = 1`.

- `insert(3, "ccccc")`: slot 1 is empty, so the result is `[]`.
- `insert(1, "aaaaa")`: slot 1 is filled; push `"aaaaa"`, `pointer` becomes 2; slot 2 is empty. Result `["aaaaa"]`.
- `insert(2, "bbbbb")`: push `"bbbbb"` and `"ccccc"`; `pointer` stops at 4. Result `["bbbbb","ccccc"]`.
- `insert(5, "eeeee")`: slot 4 is empty. Result `[]`.
- `insert(4, "ddddd")`: push `"ddddd"` and `"eeeee"`; `pointer` reaches 6, the array's length. Result `["ddddd","eeeee"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) amortized per `insert`: `pointer` only moves forward, at most `n` steps over all calls, so one call may be long but all `n` together cost O(n).
- Space: O(n) for the `values` array.

## Pitfalls

- Ids start at 1; allocate `n + 1` slots or shift by one, but do not mix the two.
- Stop at the end of the array: after the last id the loop must not read past `n`.
- Return an empty list, not `null`, when nothing can be released.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `values` | `values[id]` is the value stored for `id`, or `null` if it has not arrived |
| `pointer` | the smallest id not yet returned |
| `chunk` | the values released by this `insert` call |
| `idKey`, `value` | the pair being inserted |

narration.3: One slot per id from 1 to n; null means the value has not arrived yet.
narration.4: The next id to release is 1.
narration.8: Store the new value in its id's slot.
narration.9: Collect the values this call releases.
narration.10: Keep going while the next id to release has already arrived.
narration.11: Release that value in id order.
narration.12: Move on to the following id.
narration.14: Return the released values; empty if the next id is still missing.
